input_signals.reasoning: Working-capital investment (invt growth) alone is a weak predictor, but conditioned on negative profitability (low ib/at) it becomes a forced-inventory / distressed-liquidation indicator rather than a demand-anticipation indicator. input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose investment outlays exceed operating cash flow must fund the gap externally; when they are already highly levered, that funding is costly, dilutive, or rationed, so expected equity value is impaired relative to firms with the same gap but spare debt capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: The first leg measures the internal-funding shortfall of the investment program, the second measures the remaining balance-sheet capacity to close it. input_signals.expression: RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: The credit-relevant quantity is the total cash the firm must raise in the coming year — capital expenditure it has committed to plus debt actually maturing, less what operations will generate — and equity in firms with a large required raise is exposed to whatever terms the market imposes.

input_signals.hypothesis: Debt is ultimately serviced out of revenue, not out of book assets, so obligations measured in years of sales is the fragility metric that cannot be flattered by capitalized acquisition premia or asset write-ups; expanding capacity while owing many years of revenue is the value-destroying combination.

input_signals.name: RequirementWithCapacityOverhang
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ppent, sale), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fixed capacity carried above the firm's own historical revenue-adjusted norm is idle plant: it generates depreciation and maintenance obligations without sales, and a firm needing external cash cannot convert it quickly except at a liquidation discount.
input_signals.reasoning: This completes the test of whether own-history overhang is a general concept spanning all three asset margins — working capital, labor and fixed capital — or is specific to inventory, which matters for interpreting the leading signal as a financing-constraint mechanism rather than an inventory-anomaly variant. It also revisits the capital margin with a construction that succeeded elsewhere, after the earlier vintage-based attempt (accumulated depreciation over gross plant) produced a flat cross-sectional slope.

input_signals.name: RequirementWithDepletedOwnLiquidity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash-to-short-term-claims is a firm-specific policy variable, so what signals strain is not a low level but a level low by the firm's own standard: a firm whose liquidity buffer sits at the bottom of its five-year range while it faces a funding requirement has already spent its self-insurance.
input_signals.reasoning: Earlier cross-sectional cash-buffer conditioners either failed on the FMB slope or risked rediscovering the published cash-to-assets anomaly, and the own-history benchmark is precisely the fix, since it differences out the firm's permanent cash policy and isolates depletion. It closes the batch with the one fragility dimension that is neither a commitment nor an asset overhang but the exhaustion of the reserve that would otherwise absorb the requirement.

input_signals.name: RequirementWithMultiYearStockBuild
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose inventory days have been drifting upward year after year has a structural accumulation problem — goods entering faster than they clear, over multiple demand cycles — which is a different and more damaging state than a single high reading, and it leaves the firm least able to self-fund when cash is needed.
input_signals.reasoning:
The amplifier is the five-year *slope* of inventory days rather than the current position within that window, so it is directional and chronic rather than a level measured on a different scale: a firm sitting at the top of its range after a sharp one-year build scores high on TS_RANK but low on TREND, while a firm three years into a steady drift scores the reverse. This uses the one temporal construct the archive has never tested, and it discriminates a genuine economic question left open by the leading signal — whether the overhang that matters is an acute spike or a persistent multi-year deterioration in how fast the firm converts stock into cash.
